pumac-2007-power-01a.title: Look at the integers nearest $0$
pumac-2007-power-01a.body:
The nonzero integers closest to $0$ are $1$ and $-1$ (distance $1$). Any other nonzero integer has absolute value at least $2$.

**Answer: 2**

pumac-2007-power-01b.title: Count the vectors of norm 1
pumac-2007-power-01b.body:
A nonzero integer vector has norm $a^2+b^2+c^2\ge 1$ with equality exactly when one coordinate is $\pm1$ and the other two are $0$. That gives $3\cdot 2=6$ vectors: $(\pm1,0,0),(0,\pm1,0),(0,0,\pm1)$.

**Answer: 6**

pumac-2007-power-01c.title: Generalise the previous two parts
pumac-2007-power-01c.body:
A nonzero vector $x\in\mathbb Z^m$ has norm $\sum x_i^2\ge 1$, since some coordinate is a nonzero integer. Equality holds exactly when one coordinate is $\pm1$ and all others are $0$. Choose the coordinate ($m$ ways) and the sign ($2$ ways).

**Answer: $2m$**

pumac-2007-power-01d.title: Norms in $D_3$ are even
pumac-2007-power-01d.body:
For $x\in\mathbb Z^3$, $\sum x_i^2\equiv\sum x_i\pmod 2$, so every vector of $D_3$ has even norm. A nonzero vector therefore has norm at least $2$.

Norm $2$ means exactly two coordinates equal $\pm1$ and the third is $0$; the coordinate sum is then $0,\pm2$, which is even, so all of these are in $D_3$. Choose the zero coordinate (3 ways) and the two signs ($4$ ways): $12$ vectors.

**Answer: 12**

pumac-2007-power-01e.title: Same argument as for $D_3$
pumac-2007-power-01e.body:
As in the case $m=3$, $\sum x_i^2\equiv \sum x_i \pmod 2$, so every vector of $D_m$ has even norm and the minimal norm is at least $2$. Norm $2$ is attained by the vectors with exactly two nonzero coordinates, both $\pm1$ (their sum is even). Choose the two positions $\binom m2$ ways and the two signs $4$ ways:
$$4\binom m2 = 2m(m-1).$$

(For $m=1$, $D_1=2\mathbb Z$ has just the two minimal vectors $\pm2$.)

**Answer: $2m(m-1)$**

pumac-2007-power-02a.title: Standard basis
pumac-2007-power-02a.body: Any $x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb Z^m$ equals $\sum x_ie_i$ with integer coefficients $x_i$, and every integer combination of the $e_i$ is in $\mathbb Z^m$. So $e_1,\dots,e_m$ is a basis. ∎

pumac-2007-power-02b.title: Exhibit the basis and prove it works
pumac-2007-power-02b.body:
Take $u_1=(2,0,\dots,0)$ and $u_i=-e_{i-1}+e_i$ for $i=2,\dots,m$. Each has even coordinate sum, so each lies in $D_m$, and so does every integer combination.

Conversely let $x\in D_m$. We want integers $k_1,\dots,k_m$ with $x=\sum k_iu_i$. Comparing coordinates: coordinate $m$ gives $k_m=x_m$; coordinate $i$ ($2\le i<m$) gives $k_i-k_{i+1}=x_i$; coordinate $1$ gives $2k_1-k_2=x_1$. Hence
$$k_i=x_i+x_{i+1}+\dots+x_m\ (i\ge2),\qquad k_1=\tfrac12(x_1+k_2)=\tfrac12(x_1+\dots+x_m).$$
All $k_i$ are integers because $x_1+\dots+x_m$ is even. So $u_1,\dots,u_m$ is a basis of $D_m$. ∎

pumac-2007-power-02c.title: Describe the lattice
pumac-2007-power-02c.body:
Let $h=(\frac12,\dots,\frac12)$ and let $S$ be the set of $x\in\mathbb R^8$ whose coordinates are all in $\mathbb Z$ or all in $\mathbb Z+\frac12$, with $\sum x_i$ even. Equivalently $S=D_8\cup(D_8+h)$ (for $x$ half-odd, $x-h\in\mathbb Z^8$ with sum $\sum x_i-4$, even).

**The lattice lies in $S$.** Each basis vector is in $S$, and $S$ is closed under negation and addition: the only new case is $(a+h)+(b+h)=a+b+(1,\dots,1)$ with $a,b\in D_8$, whose coordinate sum is even because $8$ is even.

**$S$ lies in the lattice $L$.** The first seven basis vectors are the $D_7$ basis from the previous part, placed in the first seven coordinates; hence they generate every integer vector in the first seven coordinates with even sum. The vector $c=(1,1,1,1,1,1,2,0)$ has sum $8$, so $c\in L$; also $2h=(1,\dots,1)\in L$. Therefore $e_8-e_7=2h-c\in L$. Now $(2,0,\dots,0)$ and $e_i-e_{i-1}$ ($i=2,\dots,8$) all lie in $L$, and they form a basis of $D_8$, so $D_8\subseteq L$. With $h\in L$ this gives $S=D_8\cup(D_8+h)\subseteq L$. So $L=S$.

**Minimal norm.** An integer vector of $S$ has even norm ($\sum x_i^2\equiv\sum x_i$), so a nonzero one has norm $\ge2$, with equality for exactly two coordinates $\pm1$: $\binom82\cdot4=112$ vectors. A half-odd vector has every coordinate squared $\ge\frac14$, so norm $\ge2$ with equality iff all coordinates are $\pm\frac12$; the sum is $4-m$ for $m$ minus signs, so $m$ must be even: $2^7=128$ vectors. Minimal norm $2$, with $112+128=240$ minimal vectors. ∎

pumac-2007-power-02d.title: Split by parity
pumac-2007-power-02d.body:
$\supseteq$: $D_3\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$ and $(1,1,1)\in\mathbb Z^3$, so $D_3+(1,1,1)\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$.

$\subseteq$: let $x\in\mathbb Z^3$. If its coordinate sum is even, $x\in D_3$. If it is odd, then $x-(1,1,1)$ is an integer vector with sum (odd) $-3$, which is even, so $x-(1,1,1)\in D_3$ and $x\in D_3+(1,1,1)$. ∎

pumac-2007-power-02e.title: Use the description of $E_8$
pumac-2007-power-02e.body: From the previous part, $E_8$ is the set of vectors with all coordinates integers or all half-odd-integers and even coordinate sum. The integer ones form $D_8$. If $x$ has half-odd coordinates, then $x-h\in\mathbb Z^8$ and its sum is $\sum x_i-4$, which is even exactly when $\sum x_i$ is even; so such $x$ are precisely the points of $D_8+h$. Hence $E_8=D_8\cup(D_8+h)$ with $h=(\frac12,\dots,\frac12)$. ∎

pumac-2007-power-03a.title: Hexagonal packing
pumac-2007-power-03a.body:
Place equal circles so that their centres are the vertices of a tiling of the plane by equilateral triangles whose side is twice the radius. Each circle touches six neighbours. This is the densest circle packing (Thue/Fejes Tóth), with density $\pi/\sqrt{12}\approx0.9069$ (computed in part (d)).

```
   o   o   o   o
 o   o   o   o
   o   o   o   o
 o   o   o   o
```
(rows are offset by half a diameter; each $o$ is a circle centre, neighbouring circles touch).

pumac-2007-power-03b.title: Neighbouring centres are at distance 1
pumac-2007-power-03b.body: Put a circle centre at the origin. Touching circles have centres at distance $2\cdot\frac12=1$. In the hexagonal packing the six neighbours of the origin sit at the vertices of a regular hexagon of side $1$: $(1,0)$, $(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2)$, $(-\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2)$, and their negatives. Every centre is an integer combination of $v_1=(1,0)$ and $v_2=(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2)$, since these two vectors generate the whole triangular grid (the grid is tiled by the equilateral triangles with sides $v_1$, $v_2$, $v_2-v_1$). So $\{(1,0),(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2)\}$ is a basis (any rotation of it is equally good).

pumac-2007-power-03c.title: Compare with the basis from part (b)
pumac-2007-power-03c.body:
Let $a=(1,-1,0)$ and $b=(0,1,-1)$. Both lie in the plane $x+y+z=0$, and
$$|a|^2=|b|^2=2,\qquad a\cdot b=-1,\quad\text{so}\ \cos\angle(a,b)=-\tfrac12,\ \angle(a,b)=120^\circ .$$
The lattice generated by $a,b$ is the same as the lattice generated by $a$ and $a+b=(1,0,-1)$, which also has length $\sqrt2$, and the angle between $a$ and $a+b$ is $60^\circ$ (indeed $a\cdot(a+b)=1$).

Now compare with part (b): the basis $v_1=(1,0)$, $v_2=(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2)$ has two vectors of length $1$ at an angle of $60^\circ$. The similarity of the plane (a rotation followed by multiplication by $\sqrt2$) sending $v_1\mapsto a$ and $v_2\mapsto a+b$ preserves lengths up to the factor $\sqrt2$ and preserves angles, so it carries the lattice $\mathbb Zv_1+\mathbb Zv_2$ onto $\mathbb Za+\mathbb Z(a+b)=\mathbb Za+\mathbb Zb$. Hence the lattice $\mathbb Za+\mathbb Zb$ is the hexagonal lattice $A_2$ of minimal distance $\sqrt2=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}2$: circles of radius $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ centred at its points form the densest packing, and $a,b$ is a basis of it up to rotation. ∎

pumac-2007-power-03d.title: Area of one cell
pumac-2007-power-03d.body:
Each lattice point owns one cell, a parallelogram spanned by the basis vectors, of area $\left|\det\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ \frac12&\frac{\sqrt3}2\end{pmatrix}\right|=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$. The cell contains exactly one circle's worth of area, $\pi(\frac12)^2=\frac\pi4$. So the density is
$$\frac{\pi/4}{\sqrt3/2}=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt3}=\frac{\pi\sqrt3}{6}\approx0.9069.$$

pumac-2007-power-03d.title: Check with the basis of part (c)
pumac-2007-power-03d.body:
Circles of radius $\frac{\sqrt2}2$ have area $\frac\pi2$; the cell spanned by $(1,-1,0)$ and $(0,1,-1)$ has area $|(1,-1,0)\times(0,1,-1)|=|(1,1,1)|=\sqrt3$. Density $\frac{\pi/2}{\sqrt3}=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt3}$ again.

**Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt3}$**

pumac-2007-power-03e.title: Radius and cell volume
pumac-2007-power-03e.body:
The minimal norm of $D_3$ is $2$, so neighbouring centres are at distance $\sqrt2$ and the spheres have radius $\frac{\sqrt2}2$. Volume of one sphere: $\frac43\pi\left(\frac{\sqrt2}2\right)^3=\frac43\pi\cdot\frac{2\sqrt2}{8}=\frac{\pi\sqrt2}{3}$.

$D_3$ has index $2$ in $\mathbb Z^3$ (it is the even-sum half of the integer points, by part 2(d): $\mathbb Z^3=D_3\cup(D_3+(1,1,1))$), so each lattice point owns volume $2$.

Density $=\dfrac{\pi\sqrt2/3}{2}=\dfrac{\pi\sqrt2}{6}\approx0.7405$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{\pi\sqrt2}{6}$**

pumac-2007-power-04a.title: Translate perpendicularity
pumac-2007-power-04a.body:
$x\cdot v=\frac12\sum x_i$, so $x\perp v$ iff $\sum x_i=0$. Hence $E_7$ consists of the points with all coordinates in $\mathbb Z$ or all in $\mathbb Z+\frac12$ and coordinate sum exactly $0$ (the sum is then automatically even).

**Minimal vectors.** $E_7\subset E_8$ has minimal norm $\ge2$, and norm $2$ is attained, so the minimal norm is $2$. The norm-$2$ vectors of $E_8$ are $(\pm1,\pm1,0^6)$ and $(\pm\frac12)^8$ (even number of minus signs). Those with coordinate sum $0$:
- integer type: one $+1$ and one $-1$: $8\cdot7=56$;
- half-odd type: four $+\frac12$ and four $-\frac12$ (four minus signs, an even number): $\binom84=70$.

Total $56+70=126$. ∎

pumac-2007-power-04b.title: The dual is the projection of $E_8$
pumac-2007-power-04b.body:
Let $H$ be the hyperplane $\sum x_i=0$ and $\pi$ the orthogonal projection onto $H$: $\pi(y)=y-\frac{s}{8}(1,\dots,1)$ with $s=\sum y_i$.

*Claim: $E_7^*=\pi(E_8)$.* $E_8$ is integral (inner products of its vectors are integers) and unimodular (it contains $D_8$, of determinant $2$, with index $2$), hence self-dual. For $y\in E_8$ and $u\in E_7$: $\pi(y)\cdot u=y\cdot u\in\mathbb Z$, so $\pi(E_8)\subseteq E_7^*$. Conversely, let $x\in E_7^*$. $E_7=E_8\cap H$ is a primitive sublattice, so the functional $u\mapsto x\cdot u$ extends to an integer-valued functional on $E_8$; as $E_8$ is self-dual it has the form $z\mapsto y\cdot z$ with $y\in E_8$. Then $y-x\perp E_7$, so $y-x$ is a multiple of $v$ and $x=\pi(y)$.

**Norms.** Since $\pi(y)$ removes the component along $(1,\dots,1)$ (of squared length $8$), $|\pi(y)|^2=|y|^2-\frac{s^2}{8}$, where $|y|^2$ is even and $s$ is even. Adding $v$ to $y$ does not change $\pi(y)$ and changes $s$ by $4$, so we may assume $s\in\{0,2\}$ (or $-2$ equivalent to $2$).
- $s=0$: $y\in E_7$, norm $\ge2$.
- $s=2$: norm $=|y|^2-\frac12\ge2-\frac12=\frac32$, with equality iff $|y|^2=2$.

So the minimal norm is $\frac32$ (matching the given vector), and the minimal vectors are the $\pi(y)$ with $s=2$, $|y|^2=2$: $y=e_i+e_j$ ($\binom82=28$ choices) or $y=(\pm\frac12)^8$ with exactly two minus signs ($28$ choices). Different $y$ with the same $s$ have different projections, so there are $28+28=56$ minimal vectors: $\pm$ the vectors $(\frac34,\frac34,-\frac14,\dots,-\frac14)$ and permutations; indeed $(\frac14^{6},-\frac34,-\frac34)=\pi$ of $(\frac12^6,-\frac12,-\frac12)$.

**Answer: 56**

pumac-2007-power-04c.title: Lengths and angle
pumac-2007-power-04c.body: Let $u=(1,0,\dots,0,1)$ and $h=(\frac12,\dots,\frac12)$. Then $|u|^2=2$, $|h|^2=8\cdot\frac14=2$, and $u\cdot h=\frac12+\frac12=1$. So $\cos\angle(u,h)=\frac{1}{2}$: the two vectors have equal length $\sqrt2$ and the angle between them is $60^\circ$. The lattice $\mathbb Zu+\mathbb Zh$ is therefore the hexagonal lattice (as in 3(b), 3(c)), i.e. a copy of $A_2$ with minimal distance $\sqrt2$. Both $u$ and $h$ lie in $E_8$ (integer vector with sum $2$; half-odd vector with sum $4$). ∎

pumac-2007-power-04d.title: Conditions for $E_6$
pumac-2007-power-04d.body:
A vector $x\in E_8$ is perpendicular to $u$ and $h$ iff $x_1+x_8=0$ and $\sum x_i=0$, i.e. $x_1+x_8=0$ and $x_2+\dots+x_7=0$. The minimal norm of $E_6\subset E_8$ is $\ge2$, and the norm-$2$ vectors of $E_8$ satisfying the conditions are:
- integer type $\pm e_i\pm e_j$: either $x_1=x_8=0$ and $e_i-e_j$ with $i,j\in\{2,\dots,7\}$ ($6\cdot5=30$), or $x_1=-x_8=\pm1$ with everything else $0$ ($2$);
- half-odd type: $x_1=-x_8=\pm\frac12$ ($2$ choices) and three $+\frac12$, three $-\frac12$ among $x_2,\dots,x_7$ ($\binom63=20$). The number of minus signs is $1+3=4$, even, as required: $40$ vectors.

So $E_6$ has minimal norm $2$ and $30+2+40=72$ minimal vectors. ∎

pumac-2007-power-04e.title: The dual is again a projection
pumac-2007-power-04e.body:
As in the previous part, $E_6=E_8\cap V$ with $V=\{u,h\}^\perp$ primitive in the unimodular lattice $E_8$, so $E_6^*=\pi_V(E_8)$, where $\pi_V$ is orthogonal projection onto $V$.

For $y\in E_8$ put $\alpha=y\cdot u$, $\beta=y\cdot h$ (integers). The Gram matrix of $u,h$ is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, with inverse $\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$, so
$$|\pi_V(y)|^2=|y|^2-\tfrac23(\alpha^2-\alpha\beta+\beta^2).$$
Adding $u$ or $h$ to $y$ does not change $\pi_V(y)$ and changes $(\alpha,\beta)$ by $(2,1)$ or $(1,2)$. These generate a sublattice of index $3$ in $\mathbb Z^2$ (the classes are given by $\alpha+\beta\bmod3$), so we may choose $y$ with $(\alpha,\beta)\in\{(0,0),(1,0),(-1,0)\}$.
- $(0,0)$: $y\in E_6$, norm $\ge2$.
- $(\pm1,0)$: norm $=|y|^2-\frac23\ge2-\frac23=\frac43$, equality iff $|y|^2=2$.

So the minimal norm is $\frac43$, and the minimal vectors are $\pm\pi_V(y)$ with $y$ a norm-$2$ vector with $y\cdot h=0$, $y\cdot u=1$ (distinct $y$ give distinct images, since the difference of two such $y$ in the kernel $\mathbb Zu+\mathbb Zh$ must have $\alpha=\beta=0$). Count the $y$ with $y_1+y_8=1$, $\sum y_i=0$, $|y|^2=2$: integer type $e_i-e_j$ with $i\in\{1,8\}$, $j\in\{2,\dots,7\}$ ($2\cdot6=12$); half-odd type with $y_1=y_8=+\frac12$ and four minus signs among the other six ($\binom64=15$). That is $27$, so $2\cdot27=54$ minimal vectors.

Using $\pi_V(y)=y-\frac23u+\frac13h$ for $(\alpha,\beta)=(1,0)$, the $12$ integer roots give the $12$ vectors of type (ii) with positive sign pattern ($x_1=-x_8=\pm\frac12$, middle $=\pm(e_k-\frac16\mathbf 1)$ with fixed sign) and the $15$ half-odd roots give $15$ of the vectors of type (i); the negatives give the remaining ones. This is the list in the answer. ∎

pumac-2007-power-05a.title: Pair up coordinates
pumac-2007-power-05a.body: Send $(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{2m-1},x_{2m})\in\mathbb Z^{2m}$ to $(x_1+x_2i,\ \dots,\ x_{2m-1}+x_{2m}i)\in\mathbb C^m$. Each complex coordinate ranges over all Gaussian integers independently, so the image is exactly $G^m$, the lattice with the standard basis $e_1=(1,0,\dots,0),\dots,e_m=(0,\dots,0,1)$ over $G$. (Norms agree: $\sum|z_j|^2=\sum x_k^2$.) ∎

pumac-2007-power-05b.title: Describe $\Lambda$ and find its minimal vectors
pumac-2007-power-05b.body:
Let $E=\mathbb Z[\omega]$ and $\theta=\sqrt3\,i=1+2\omega$ (so $|\theta|^2=3$). A general element of $\Lambda$ is $a(\theta,0,0)+b(1,-1,0)+c(1,0,-1)=(a\theta+b+c,\ -b,\ -c)$ with $a,b,c\in E$. So $z_2,z_3\in E$ are arbitrary and $z_1+z_2+z_3=a\theta$. Hence
$$\Lambda=\{z\in E^3:\ z_1+z_2+z_3\in\theta E\}.$$
Since $\omega\equiv1\pmod\theta$, every element of $E$ is congruent to $0,1$ or $-1$ mod $\theta E$ (index $3$), and the units $\pm1,\pm\omega,\pm\omega^2$ are $\equiv\pm1$.

The norms of Eisenstein integers $|a+b\omega|^2=a^2-ab+b^2$ are $0,1,3,4,\dots$ (never $2$). So a vector of $E^3$ of norm $2$ has exactly two nonzero coordinates, both units, and a vector of norm $1$ has a single unit coordinate. A single unit coordinate has $z_1+z_2+z_3\equiv\pm1\not\equiv0$, so it is not in $\Lambda$: the minimal norm is $2$. A norm-$2$ vector $(u,u',0)$ (in any positions) lies in $\Lambda$ iff $u+u'\equiv0\pmod\theta$, i.e. $u,u'$ have opposite residues $\pm1$. Count: $3$ choices for the zero coordinate, $6$ choices of $u$, then $3$ choices of $u'$ with the opposite sign class: $3\cdot6\cdot3=54$ minimal vectors.

pumac-2007-power-05b.title: Equivalence with $E_6^*$
pumac-2007-power-05b.body:
Six of the minimal vectors of $\Lambda$ are
$w_1=(0,\omega,-\omega)$, $w_2=(\omega^2,0,-\omega)$, $w_3=(0,\omega,-\omega^2)$, $w_4=(-\omega,\omega,0)$, $w_5=(-\omega^2,0,1)$, $w_6=(-\omega,\omega^2,0)$.
With the real inner product $\mathrm{Re}\sum z_j\overline{z_j'}$, their Gram matrix is
$$G=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&\frac12&1&\frac12&-\frac12\\1&2&-\frac12&\frac12&-\frac12&\frac12\\\frac12&-\frac12&2&1&\frac12&-\frac12\\1&\frac12&1&2&-\frac12&\frac12\\\frac12&-\frac12&\frac12&-\frac12&2&-\frac12\\-\frac12&\frac12&-\frac12&\frac12&-\frac12&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det G=\tfrac{243}{64}.$$
The real lattice underlying $\Lambda$ has basis $v_j,\omega v_j$ ($j=1,2,3$), whose Gram determinant is also $\frac{243}{64}$; the $w_k$ lie in $\Lambda$ and have the same Gram determinant, hence they form a basis of $\Lambda$ (a sublattice of index $d$ has determinant $d^2$ times larger).

In $E_6^*$ (4(e)), the six minimal vectors
$(\frac12,-\frac16,-\frac16,\frac56,-\frac16,-\frac16,-\frac16,-\frac12)$, $(\frac12,\frac16,\frac16,\frac16,-\frac56,\frac16,\frac16,-\frac12)$, $(0,-\frac23,\frac13,\frac13,\frac13,-\frac23,\frac13,0)$, $(\frac12,\frac16,\frac16,\frac16,\frac16,-\frac56,\frac16,-\frac12)$, $(0,-\frac23,\frac13,\frac13,\frac13,\frac13,-\frac23,0)$, $(0,\frac23,\frac23,-\frac13,-\frac13,-\frac13,-\frac13,0)$
have Gram matrix exactly $\frac23G$ and Gram determinant $\frac13=\det E_6^*$ (as $\det E_6=3$), so they form a basis of $E_6^*$. Sending the $k$-th basis vector to $w_k$ is a linear map multiplying all lengths by $\sqrt{3/2}$, i.e. a rotation composed with a scaling, taking $E_6^*$ onto $\Lambda$. Hence $\Lambda$ is $E_6^*$ (up to rotation and scale); the $54$ minimal vectors of both lattices correspond. ∎
